overview: This unit covers predicate logic (Prädikatlogik), logical connectives (Junktoren), quantifiers (Quantoren), and valid inferences (gültige Schlussfolgerungen). Truth tables (Wahrheitstabellen) and diagrams help evaluate compound statements; bounded quantifiers (beschränkte Quantoren) express claims about selected objects. Examples involving syllogisms (Syllogismen), systems of equations, and inference forms show how to check conclusions and refute invalid inferences with countermodels (Gegenmodelle). Direct proof (direkter Beweis), contraposition (Kontraposition), proof by contradiction (Widerspruchsbeweis), and equivalence proof (Äquivalenzbeweis) are central proof strategies (Beweisstrategien); induction (Induktion) is mentioned as another strategy.

entries.short: Predicate logic describes properties of objects and relationships between them using variables and quantifiers.
entries.explanation: In predicate logic, statements can depend on which objects are assigned to variables. Predicates express properties or relationships, and quantifiers state whether something holds for every object or for at least one object. This makes it possible to formulate general statements that go beyond individual, fully specified statements.
entries.example: With the integers as the domain and the predicates G(x) for “x is even” and Z(x) for “x is an integer,” ∀x (G(x) ⇒ Z(x)) expresses that every even integer is an integer.
pitfalls: A statement form with a free variable has no fixed truth value until the variable is assigned a value.
related: Statement forms and predicates (Aussageform und Prädikat)
Domain and variable binding (Grundmenge und Variablenbindung)
entries.heading: 1. Prädikatlogik und Aussageformen

entries.short: A predicate is a statement form whose truth value depends on the objects assigned to its variables.
entries.explanation: A statement form such as “x is an integer” contains a variable and acquires a definite truth value only once a value is assigned to it. A predicate can also contain several variables and thereby express a relationship between objects. Variables can be assigned specific objects or bound by quantifiers.
entries.example: For P(x) = “x is even,” P(4) is true and P(5) is false.
pitfalls: A statement form is not automatically true or false while its free variables remain unassigned.
entries.heading: 1. Prädikatlogik und Aussageformen

entries.short: The domain specifies which objects variables may denote; quantifiers bind variables.
entries.explanation: The domain and the meanings of the predicates must be specified in order to evaluate a statement. A variable is free if no quantifier binds it; free variables must be assigned values for the statement form to have a definite truth value. A bound variable lies within the scope of a quantifier such as ∀ or ∃.
entries.example: √2 is a permissible assignment for a variable whose domain is ℝ, but not for one whose domain is ℚ.
pitfalls: A statement can change its truth value when the domain changes.
A formula can contain bound and free variables at the same time.
related: Rational and real numbers (Rationale und reelle Zahlen)
entries.heading: 1. Prädikatlogik und Aussageformen

entries.short: Connectives combine statements, and a truth table shows the result for every possible assignment.
entries.explanation: The connectives include negation ¬A, conjunction A ∧ B, disjunction A ∨ B, the conditional (Konditional) A ⇒ B, and the biconditional (Bikonditional) A ⇔ B. In the lecture notes, w denotes “true” and f denotes “false.” The logical OR is inclusive, so it is true when at least one component statement is true; a truth table systematically lists all assignments.
entries.example: For A = f and B = w, A ∨ B = w and A ⇔ B = f.
pitfalls: Logical OR is inclusive unless an exclusive OR (Exklusives Oder) is explicitly intended.
For ¬A, the truth value of another statement B does not affect the result.
related: If-Then-Else as a logical connective (If-Then-Else als logische Verknüpfung)
entries.heading: 2. Junktoren und ihre Wahrheitsbereiche

entries.short: Exclusive OR is true exactly when one of two statements is true and the other is false.
entries.explanation: “Either A or B” in its usual exclusive sense denotes a connective that is false when both statements have the same truth value. It is true when one statement is true and the other is false. It can, for example, be expressed by the formula (A ∧ ¬B) ∨ (¬A ∧ B).
entries.example: If A = f and B = w, exclusive OR is true; if A = w and B = w, it is false.
pitfalls: Inclusive OR, A ∨ B, is also true when both component statements are true.
entries.heading: 2. Junktoren und ihre Wahrheitsbereiche

entries.short: The conditional A ⇒ B is false exactly when A is true and B is false.
entries.explanation: A ⇒ B is read as “If A, then B.” If A is true, B must also be true; if A is false, the conditional is true regardless of B. In propositional logic, it specifies a truth condition, not causation or temporal sequence.
entries.example: “If pigs can fly, then π is irrational” is true when its antecedent is false.
pitfalls: A false antecedent does not make the conditional false.
A conditional by itself asserts no factual connection between its antecedent and consequent.
related: Sufficient and necessary conditions (Hinreichende und notwendige Bedingungen)
entries.heading: Konditional und Bikonditional

entries.short: A ⇔ B is true when A and B have the same truth value.
entries.explanation: A ⇔ B is read as “A if and only if B.” The biconditional is equivalent to the conjunction of both directions: (A ⇒ B) ∧ (B ⇒ A). Thus, it requires both that A implies B and that B implies A.
entries.example: For real x, x + 2 = 5 ⇔ x = 3.
pitfalls: Proving only one of the two implications is not enough to establish a biconditional.
related: Iff and logical equivalence (gdw und logische Gleichwertigkeit)
entries.heading: Konditional und Bikonditional

entries.short: The If-Then-Else connective returns the truth value of B when A is true and that of C when A is false.
entries.explanation: For “If A, then B, else C,” I(A,B,C) ≡ (A ∧ B) ∨ (¬A ∧ C). Equivalently, I(A,B,C) ≡ (A ⇒ B) ∧ (¬A ⇒ C). The special case “if A, then B, else true” corresponds to A ⇒ B; “if A, then B, else not B” corresponds to A ⇔ B.
entries.example: For A = f, B = w, and C = f, the result is false because when A is false, the else branch C determines the result.
pitfalls: When A is false, C determines the result; B is irrelevant.
related: Difference from program branching (Unterschied zur Verzweigung im Programm)
entries.heading: If-Then-Else als logische Verknüpfung

entries.term: Matching truth regions and Venn diagrams (Wahrheitsbereiche und Venn-Diagramme zuordnen)
entries.short: To check a diagram for a logical statement, evaluate its regions as assignments of truth values to the statements.
entries.explanation: Each region represents a combination in which A, B, and, where applicable, C are true or false. Read off these truth values for a region, evaluate the formula using the corresponding row of the table, and compare the result with the region’s color. Repeat for the remaining regions. For a conditional, only A ∧ ¬B is false; a general If-Then-Else may be false for several combinations.
entries.example: For A ⇒ B, the part inside A and outside B is the only false region.
pitfalls: In a diagram with three statements, a region may combine several table rows if one statement does not affect the formula.
related: Venn and Euler diagrams (Venn- und Euler-Diagramme)
entries.heading: Ein Venn-Diagramm einer Aussage zuordnen

entries.short: A logical If-Then-Else combines truth values, whereas a program executes instructions depending on a condition.
entries.explanation: In a programming language, a branch is usually preceded by a condition A. The branches contain instructions that are executed depending on the condition’s truth value. By contrast, the logical connective evaluates the truth values of A, B, and C and itself returns a truth value.
entries.example: In Python, `if A: print("b") else: print("c")` executes one of the two statements depending on A.
pitfalls: Instructions in program branches are not automatically the truth values B and C in a logical formula.
entries.heading: Unterschied zur Verzweigung im Programm

entries.short: A propositional formula is logically valid if it is true under every assignment.
entries.explanation: Logical validity means that no possible assignment of the statements in a formula makes it false. A formula A ⇒ B is not logically valid just by virtue of its form, since it is false when A = w and B = f. For statement forms, the domain of objects under consideration must also be specified.
entries.example: A ∨ ¬A is true under every assignment.
pitfalls: A single assignment that makes a formula true is not enough to show logical validity.
The logical validity of a formula and the validity of an inference (Gültigkeit eines Schlusses) are related but distinct concepts.
entries.heading: 3. Gültigkeit, hinreichende und notwendige Bedingungen

entries.short: If A ⇒ B holds, A is sufficient for B and B is necessary for A.
entries.explanation: A is sufficient for B if A is enough to infer B. B is necessary for A if A cannot hold without B. Set-theoretically, the truth set of A is then contained in the truth set of B: {x | A(x)} ⊆ {x | B(x)}. If both directions hold, each statement is necessary and sufficient for the other.
entries.example: For real x, “x/2 is an integer” is sufficient for “x is an integer”; x being an integer is necessary for x/2 to be an integer.
pitfalls: In A ⇒ B, A is sufficient and B is necessary; reversing the direction swaps these roles.
entries.heading: Allgemeine Begriffe

entries.short: “Iff” means “if and only if,” and logically equivalent statement forms have the same truth value under every assignment.
entries.explanation: “A iff B” stands for the biconditional A ⇔ B. Two statement forms are logically equivalent if their truth values agree under every assignment. The lecture notes use “GDW” to indicate equivalence and “syn” for synonymy or equivalence.
entries.example: A ⇔ B and (A ⇒ B) ∧ (B ⇒ A) are logically equivalent.
pitfalls: Equivalence requires agreement under every assignment, not just in one example.
entries.heading: „gdw“, „GDW“ und gleichbedeutende Aussageformen

entries.short: A mathematical theorem or lemma is a claim whose validity must be proved under specified assumptions.
entries.explanation: A theorem is a mathematical claim, often in the form “If A, then B.” A lemma is also a claim to be proved and often serves as an intermediate step in a further proof. The claim holds within its specified domain and under its assumptions.
entries.example: For real x, the claim x/2 ∈ ℤ ⇒ x ∈ ℤ is a conditional whose validity must be justified in the stated domain.
pitfalls: The form “A implies B” is not automatically true for arbitrary meanings of A and B.
entries.heading: Allgemeine Begriffe

entries.short: A bounded quantifier makes a claim only about objects that satisfy a specified restriction.
entries.explanation: The universal quantifier ∀ means “for all,” and the existential quantifier ∃ means “there exists at least one.” “All objects satisfying R satisfy P” means ∀x (R(x) ⇒ P(x)); R is the restriction and P is the required property. A bounded existential claim can, for example, be written as ∃x (R(x) ∧ P(x)).
entries.example: “All integers divisible by 4 are even” can be written as ∀x (D₄(x) ⇒ G(x)) when the domain is ℤ.
pitfalls: “Some” means at least one object and does not rule out additional objects with the property.
A universal statement does not claim that any object satisfies the restriction.
related: Four forms of bounded quantifiers (Vier Formen beschränkter Quantoren)
entries.heading: Alle Objekte mit R haben auch P

entries.short: The four forms express whether all, not all, some, or no objects satisfying R have property P.
entries.explanation: “All R are P” means ∀x (R(x) ⇒ P(x)); “not all R are P” means ∃x (R(x) ∧ ¬P(x)). “Some R are P” means ∃x (R(x) ∧ P(x)); “no R is P” means ∀x (R(x) ⇒ ¬P(x)). A dot in a quantifier diagram indicates an asserted witness, while a shaded region is empty or excluded.
entries.example: “Some positive real numbers have square 4” is true, since x = 2 has both properties.
pitfalls: “Not all R are P” means that at least one R is not P; it does not mean that no R is P.
entries.heading: Die vier wichtigen Formen

entries.short: Venn diagrams show all membership combinations, whereas Euler diagrams represent specific relationships between sets.
entries.explanation: A Venn diagram divides the objects under consideration into regions for every combination of membership and non-membership in the sets. An Euler diagram represents specific relationships between sets through the placement of its curves, for example by drawing one circle entirely inside another. In quantifier diagrams, a shaded region can be marked as empty or excluded.
entries.example: If every A-object is also a B-object, an Euler diagram can show circle A entirely inside circle B.
pitfalls: A Venn diagram also shows combinations that must be empty because of a specific relationship between sets.
In everyday usage, “Venn diagram” is sometimes used as a general term for set diagrams.
related: Matching truth regions and Venn diagrams
entries.heading: Venn- und Euler-Diagramme

entries.short: A witness satisfies an existential claim, and a counterexample refutes a universal claim.
entries.explanation: A witness is an object that satisfies the property in an existential claim. A counterexample violates a universal claim and is also a witness for its negation. An existential claim can be proved by providing a suitable witness; a universal claim requires a general argument covering all objects under consideration.
entries.example: The number 1 is a counterexample to “All integers are even,” since 1 is an integer and is odd.
pitfalls: A suitable example does not in general prove a universal claim.
A single unsuccessful candidate does not refute an existential claim.
entries.heading: Zeugen und Gegenbeispiele

entries.short: When negating a quantifier, “for all” becomes “there exists,” and the property is negated.
entries.explanation: We have ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). It follows also that ∀x P(x) ≡ ¬∃x ¬P(x) and ∃x P(x) ≡ ¬∀x ¬P(x). Thus, negating a universal statement says that at least one counterexample exists.
entries.example: “Not all integers are even” means: “There is an integer that is not even.”
pitfalls: Negation requires both switching the quantifier and negating the property.
entries.heading: Quantoren durch Negation ausdrücken

entries.short: The truth value of a quantified statement may depend on whether its domain is ℚ or ℝ.
entries.explanation: The rational numbers ℚ are a subset of the real numbers ℝ, and some real numbers are not rational. Therefore, the same property can have different truth values over ℚ and ℝ. For example, x² ≠ 2 holds for every rational x but not for every real x, since √2 is real and its square is 2.
entries.example: ∃x ∈ ℚ: x² = 2 is false, whereas ∃x ∈ ℝ: x² = 2 is true.
pitfalls: √2 is not a permissible witness for an existential claim whose domain is ℚ.
entries.heading: Rationale und reelle Zahlen unterscheiden

entries.term: Direction of a conditional (Richtung eines Konditionals)
entries.short: A conditional specifies which antecedent leads to the consequent; the reverse direction must be checked separately.
entries.explanation: A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A are not generally equivalent. For real x, x = √2 ⇒ x² = 2, but the reverse statement must account for both solutions: x² = 2 ⇒ (x = −√2 ∨ x = √2). Swapping the antecedent and consequent can therefore produce a false statement.
entries.example: “x is a solution of x² = 2” does not imply that x = √2, since x = −√2 is also a solution.
pitfalls: The converse of a true conditional is not automatically true.
entries.heading: Die Richtung eines Konditionals beachten

entries.short: A syllogism is an inference in which a conclusion is derived from premises.
entries.explanation: In its classical Aristotelian form, a syllogism has exactly two premises (Prämissen) and a conclusion (Konklusion), often using statements of the forms “all,” “some,” or “none.” Validity depends on the structure of the inference, not on whether the names used refer to real objects. An inference is valid if true premises do not permit a false conclusion.
entries.example: All bandersnatches are borogoves; all borogoves are slithy; therefore, all bandersnatches are slithy.
pitfalls: The truth of the conclusion alone does not show that it follows from the premises.
entries.heading: 5. Syllogismen und gültige Schlussfolgerungen

entries.short: An inference is valid if there is no assignment under which all the premises are true and the conclusion is false.
entries.explanation: Validity describes the logical relationship between premises and conclusion. It does not guarantee that the premises are actually true; it guarantees that the conclusion must be true if all the premises are true. An inference is invalid as soon as a countermodel with true premises and a false conclusion exists.
entries.example: “All pigs can fly” and “Miss Piggy is a pig” validly imply “Miss Piggy can fly,” even though the first premise is actually false.
pitfalls: Invalidity does not mean that the conclusion is always false, only that it does not necessarily follow from the premises.
The validity of an inference is not the same as the logical validity of a formula.
entries.heading: 5. Syllogismen und gültige Schlussfolgerungen

entries.short: Premises are assumed starting statements in an inference, and the conclusion is the statement derived from them.
entries.explanation: An inference with premises P₁ and P₂ and conclusion C can be written as a fraction, with P₁ and P₂ above a horizontal line and C below it. This notation makes the structure of an inference visible. By itself, it does not show whether the inference is valid.
entries.example: Writing (A ⇒ B, A) above the inference bar and B below it represents modus ponens (Modus ponens, Modus tollens und Verkettung von Konditionalen).
pitfalls: Merely writing a conclusion below a line does not prove that the inference rule is valid.
related: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals
entries.heading: Prämissen und Konklusion

entries.term: Pigs and Miss Piggy (Schweine und Miss Piggy)
entries.short: The pig examples show that an inference’s validity depends on its logical form.
entries.explanation: From “All pigs can fly” and “Miss Piggy is a pig,” it validly follows that Miss Piggy can fly. This does not follow from “Some pigs can fly” and “Miss Piggy is a pig,” since the flying pig could be a different one. By contrast, “Some pigs can fly” and “All pigs are animals” imply that some animals can fly.
entries.example: A countermodel to the invalid inference contains a flying pig d and a non-flying Miss Piggy.
pitfalls: “Some pigs can fly” does not mean that every pig can fly.
entries.heading: Schweine, Fliegen und Miss Piggy

entries.term: Children, good behavior, and gifts (Kinder, Benehmen und Geschenke)
entries.short: The examples about children distinguish valid inferences from converses that admit countermodels.
entries.explanation: If every child who behaves well receives a gift, and Lea behaves well, it follows that Lea receives a gift. If some children behave well and all well-behaved children receive a gift, it follows that some children receive a gift. A gift for Lea does not imply that she behaved well; likewise, “Some well-behaved children receive gifts” and “Lea behaves well” do not imply that Lea receives a gift.
entries.example: For the invalid inference from Lea receiving a gift to her having behaved well, Lea could receive a gift even though she did not behave well.
pitfalls: A general rule about a group does not automatically establish that every member of the group has the stated property.
entries.heading: Vier eigene Beispiele: Kinder, Benehmen und Geschenke

entries.term: Inferences from a system of linear equations (Schlussfolgerungen bei einem linearen Gleichungssystem)
entries.short: In the elimination method, equations are multiplied and added so that one variable cancels.
entries.explanation: For 3x + 4y = 0 and −2x + 3y = 17, you can multiply the first equation by 2 and the second by 3. Adding them gives 17y = 51, so y = 3; substituting into the first equation gives x = −4. Checking both equations confirms the solution, and the derivation shows that every common solution pair must have these values.
entries.example: (x, y) = (−4, 3) satisfies both equations: 3(−4) + 4(3) = 0 and −2(−4) + 3(3) = 17.
pitfalls: A transformation must be applied to both sides of the equation.
A proposed solution should be checked in every original equation.
entries.heading: 6. Schlussfolgerungen bei einem linearen Gleichungssystem

entries.term: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals
entries.short: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals are valid forms of inference.
entries.explanation: Modus ponens has the form: from A ⇒ B and A, infer B. Modus tollens has the form: from A ⇒ B and ¬B, infer ¬A. By chaining conditionals, A ⇒ B and B ⇒ C imply A ⇒ C.
entries.example: If a code is accepted, access is granted; if access is granted, a confirmation appears; therefore, an accepted code leads to a confirmation.
pitfalls: Modus tollens requires ¬B as its second premise.
Swapping the antecedent and consequent is not one of these valid rules.
entries.heading: 7. Quantorenfreie Schlussformen

entries.short: A countermodel to an inference makes all its premises true and its conclusion false.
entries.explanation: To show that an inference form is invalid, it is enough to give an assignment under which all the premises are true and the conclusion is false. For example, A does not necessarily follow from A ⇒ B and B: when A = f and B = w, both premises are true but the conclusion A is false. This assignment refutes the claimed validity.
entries.example: In the gift example, Lea can receive a gift without having behaved well.
pitfalls: A case with a false premise does not refute the validity of an inference.
entries.heading: Ein Gegenbeispiel entlarvt einen ungültigen Schluss

entries.short: Proof strategies provide systematic ways to justify a mathematical claim.
entries.explanation: In a direct proof, derive the claim directly from the assumption. With contraposition, prove the equivalent statement ¬B ⇒ ¬A; with proof by contradiction, assume the negation of the claim and derive a contradiction. To prove a biconditional, show both directions or give a chain of equivalent statements. Induction is mentioned as another strategy.
entries.example: To prove A ⇔ B, show A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A.
pitfalls: A proof strategy does not replace justification of the individual logical steps.
This unit only mentions induction as a strategy; it does not give a method or example.
entries.heading: 8. Übliche Beweisstrategien

entries.short: For a direct proof of A ⇒ B, assume A and derive B from it.
entries.explanation: The proof starts from the assumption and uses definitions, known facts, and valid transformations until the claim follows. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, x, 2 − x, and 2 + x are nonnegative. Therefore, −x³ + 4x + 1 = x(2 − x)(2 + x) + 1 ≥ 1 > 0, which proves the inequality for all x in the interval.
pitfalls: The assumption must not be silently replaced with a stronger one.
entries.heading: Direkter Beweis: eine Ungleichung

entries.short: A ⇒ B is logically equivalent to ¬B ⇒ ¬A.
entries.explanation: In a proof by contraposition, instead of proving the original implication, prove “If B does not hold, then A does not hold.” For universal statements, correspondingly, ∀x (P(x) ⇒ Q(x)) ⇔ ∀x (¬Q(x) ⇒ ¬P(x)). For integers n, the contrapositive of “If 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd” is shown as follows: if n = 2k is even, then 3n + 2 = 2(3k + 1) is even.
entries.example: From “n even ⇒ 3n + 2 even,” contraposition gives “3n + 2 odd ⇒ n odd.”
pitfalls: Contraposition negates both statements and swaps their roles; merely swapping them is not contraposition.
related: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals
entries.heading: Kontraposition

entries.short: In a proof by contradiction, assume the negation of the claim and derive a contradiction.
entries.explanation: To prove a statement A, assume ¬A and show that this leads to a contradiction. To prove “If 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd,” you can assume that n is even and write n = 2k. Then 3n + 2 = 2(3k + 1) is even, contradicting the assumption that it is odd.
entries.example: Assuming n is even when 3n + 2 is odd leads to the same expression being even.
pitfalls: The contradiction must be derived from the assumed negation and the available assumptions.
entries.heading: Widerspruch

entries.short: To prove A ⇔ B, show both implications or transform the statements into each other using valid steps.
entries.explanation: A biconditional holds exactly when both A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A hold. You can prove the two directions separately or give a sequence of transformations that are valid in each direction. This shows that the statements have the same truth value or the same solutions.
entries.example: For real x, x + 2 = 5 ⇔ x = 3, since the equation can be transformed in both directions by adding or subtracting 2.
pitfalls: A transformation that preserves only one direction is not enough to establish an equivalence.
entries.heading: Äquivalenz beweisen

entries.short: Induction is mentioned in this unit as another proof strategy.
entries.explanation: The lecture notes list induction as a strategy but include neither a worked method nor an example here. This unit therefore records only that induction is among the standard proof strategies.
pitfalls: This section of the unit does not explain any steps of induction.
entries.heading: Induktion
